ABF Freight employees discovered suspected narcotics inside a shipment from Los Angeles to Dayton, Ohio. Workers opened a package addressed to Douglas Bennett and contacted law enforcement Feb. 2, 2026. The discovery triggered a federal investigation involving cocaine, fentanyl, methamphetamine and marijuana. Four men subsequently pleaded guilty in connection with the trafficking conspiracy.
Federal court records identify Commonwealth Freight as the listed shipper. The cargo arrived at an ABF Freight distribution center in Dayton before employees alerted authorities. Drug Enforcement Administration agents conducted preliminary testing and obtained a federal search warrant. The government’s sentencing memorandum does not explain why workers initially opened the package.
Investigators discovered 119 brick-shaped packages containing cocaine and fentanyl across two pallets of freight. Laboratory testing confirmed approximately 118 kilograms (260 pounds) of cocaine and 1 kilogram (2.2 pounds) of fentanyl. Agents also recovered about 170 pounds of methamphetamine and 80 pounds of marijuana. DEA agents estimated the shipment’s combined street value at approximately $1.5 million, according to a federal sentencing memorandum.
Federal court records include photographs of cash found on a defendant’s cellphone (left) and narcotics seized from a commercial freight shipment in Dayton, Ohio (right). (Photos: U.S. Department of Justice, court filing)
FreightWaves previously reported a separate trafficking case involving unsuspecting trucking companies transporting cocaine from California. That investigation also demonstrated how criminal organizations can exploit commercial transportation networks. In the Dayton case, workers discovered the suspected drugs before their scheduled collection. Federal agents subsequently removed the narcotics and monitored the pickup.
Suspects collect two pallets from distribution center
DEA agents obtained tracking warrants and established surveillance at the Dayton warehouse Feb. 3, 2026. Mark Lane and Roderic Searcy arrived in a white Mercedes van to collect the shipment. Searcy presented warehouse employees with a fraudulent identification card bearing the name Douglas Bennett. The pair collected two pallets before departing the distribution facility.
A gray Honda Civic followed the Mercedes van after the pickup. Jason Heath drove, with Craig Worthen occupying the passenger seat. Both vehicles traveled to a residence on Basore Road in Dayton. Investigators watched the four men gather behind the property and open the freight.
Shortly afterward, the suspects attempted to leave the residence in their respective vehicles. Heath tried maneuvering the Honda around law enforcement vehicles but became stuck in snow. Agents arrested all four defendants following the attempted departure. Subsequent searches uncovered additional Commonwealth Freight shipping labels inside the Honda Civic.
Investigators examined Worthen’s cellphone following his arrest. Records revealed searches for ABF Freight’s Dayton terminal dating to Jan. 31, 2026. Agents also discovered a photograph depicting stacks of cash, created Jan. 19, 2026. Federal authorities seized $5,140 in cash and three cellular devices from Worthen during his arrest.
FreightWaves previously reported a separate DEA investigation involving more than 2,000 pounds of methamphetamine concealed inside a commercial cabbage shipment in Texas. Both investigations involved substantial narcotics quantities moving through commercial freight operations. However, the Dayton case involved an attempted pickup using fraudulent identification. The court records provide no explanation for how the shipment originally entered the transportation network.
One defendant sentenced, three await punishment
A federal grand jury indicted Heath, Searcy, Worthen and Lane in February 2026. Prosecutors charged the defendants with conspiring to possess controlled substances with intent to distribute. The case proceeded in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio. All four defendants eventually entered guilty pleas.
Worthen received an 11-year federal prison sentence in September, below the government’s requested 14-year term. His attorneys sought the mandatory minimum of 10 years, describing his involvement as an attempt to make quick money. The probation department recommended 11 years, matching the sentence the court ultimately imposed. Heath, Lane and Searcy also pleaded guilty and await sentencing.
The Justice Department announced Heath’s guilty plea Nov. 13 . The announcement did not identify the freight carrier involved in the investigation. However, a September sentencing memorandum reviewed by FreightWaves identifies ABF Freight as the carrier. The filing provides additional details about the investigation that the Justice Department’s announcement omitted.
FreightWaves contacted ABF Freight, an ArcBest subsidiary, seeking clarification about the discovery. In a statement to FreightWaves, ArcBest responded, “ArcBest and ABF Freight prioritize the safety and security of our employees, our customers and their freight. We partner with law enforcement as appropriate and remain committed to operating responsibly and doing what’s right.” The company did not explain what prompted employees to open the shipment. Federal prosecutors did not respond to separate questions before publication.
Why It Matters
The case highlights the importance of employee vigilance in detecting criminal activity within commercial freight networks. Suspicious shipments can move through legitimate transportation operations without the carrier’s knowledge. Identifying irregularities before cargo reaches its intended recipients can give investigators an opportunity to intervene.

AngloGold Ashanti plans to spend $2.5 billion to build its Quebradona copper project in Colombia. Credit: AngloGold Ashanti
Posted By: Henry Lazenby November 18, 2026
AngloGold Ashanti (NYSE: AU; JSE: ANG) plans to spend $2.5 billion (C$3.6 billion) to build its Quebradona copper project in Colombia if it secures an environmental licence that has eluded the company since its first application in 2019.
The underground project, about 60 km southwest of Antioquia’s capital, Medellín, could produce about 80,000 tonnes of copper a year and generate about $1.5 billion in annual exports, AngloGold said Tuesday at an investment event in New York.
“We are confident that, once the environmental approvals are obtained, the project will move towards the start of construction in 2028,” Colombian Vice-President José Manuel Restrepo said in a statement issued in Spanish by AngloGold’s local unit.
That timetable hinges in part on a 2025 order that created a temporary protected area covering the project and bars new environmental licences for mining in the zone while it’s in force. The restriction is due to run into mid-2028. AngloGold challenged the order in court and wrote down $98 million in project costs that year.
AngloGold shares fell 7.9% to $78.01 Wednesday afternoon in New York amid global declines in mining and metals stocks. That valued the company at about $39.5 billion.
Permitting question
AngloGold CEO Alberto Calderón told Colombia’s Blu Radio on Wednesday that he expects the licensing process to take 12 to 18 months. AngloGold could spend about $2 billion in the first two years of construction if it secures the licence, he said.
Colombia’s environmental licensing agency shelved the application in 2021 after identifying gaps in the company’s studies, including on groundwater, tailings storage and potential ground subsidence. The National Mining Agency in August extended exploration to December 2027, giving AngloGold time to complete more geological, environmental and water studies. The company has begun consulting communities for a new environmental impact study.
Quebradona hosts 120 million probable tonnes grading 1.23% copper for 1.47 million tonnes of contained metal, according to AngloGold’s year-end 2025 estimate. The planned plant would produce a copper concentrate with gold and silver as byproducts.

This Fully-Equipped Camper Van Offers Self-Sufficiency, Year-Round Capability, and a Homey Interior
28 photos
Photo: Vancini Conversions
Though there are countless ways to get out into nature and explore the outdoors, camper van travel remains the ultimate form of freedom. One of the main reasons people love camper vans is their flexibility. Whether you’re into weekend escapes, boondocking adventures, or sports trips, a van conversion offers a comfortable and versatile base camp that lets you enjoy all of those hobbies you love.
With over ten years of van conversion experience, Ontario-based Vancini Conversions knows best how to turn a regular cargo van into a home on wheels. The company is known for building bespoke camper vans tailored to your travel style and needs, but most of their builds end up being fully-equipped all-rounders that offer high living comfort in compact dimensions. Their latest build is no exception.
Based on a 2026 Mercedes-Benz Sprinter 170 AWD , this Vancini Conversions camper van balances ruggedness and off-grid capability with a comfortable interior that offers all the essential amenities for life on the road. It is designed to give you the freedom to roll around in a self-contained home on wheels that makes the most of the available space and comes equipped with practical accessories and nifty storage solutions that let you bring along all the equipment you need for your adventures.
It’s one of those builds that are overflowing with high-end features both inside and outside, but everything is neatly integrated and organized, so it remains airy, livable, and effortless to operate.
Built to take you anywhere, anytime, this Sprinter camper van rides on upgraded Black Rhino Arsenal rims wrapped in BFGoodrich KO3 all-terrain tires that offer rugged grip for off-road trips. For smoother rides on less-traveled routes, it has been equipped with a Van Compass 2.3 suspension kit that adds front and rear adjustable shocks and Deaver 8” leaf springs at the rear.
Photo: Vancini Conversions The van’s exterior is finished in Steel Blue and comes with a series of practical accessories, such as Atlas Roadcamp side steps, exterior storage lockers, and a Flatline Van Co. spare tire carrier at the rear, with RotopaX fuel storage mounted on it. On the driver’s side, a Flatline Van Co. ladder and surfboard hooks offer roof access and an efficient way to carry surfboards.
Up on the roof, the team installed a standard Flatline Van Co. roof rack that holds 400 watts of solar panels, along with a Fiamma F45S awning for some weather-protected space next to the van.
Stepping inside, we discover a comfortable habitat for two people with a modern aesthetic that combines natural materials with warm tones. The layout takes full advantage of the available square footage and includes a raised platform rear bed with a huge garage underneath, a well-equipped kitchen, a built-in bench, and ample storage solutions. There is no internal bathroom in this conversion, but a portable cassette toilet and an outdoor shower for easy cleanups will take care of the travelers’ sanitary needs.
Photo: Vancini Conversions With no formal divider between the cab and the rear of the van, the interior feels quite open, and the living space also benefits from Mercedes-Benz factory swivel seats, which rotate to become extra seating space. These swivel seats even pair with small tables to provide makeshift workspaces.
The ambiance is really cozy, with the materials used playing a key role in creating an inviting atmosphere. The team used a combination of clear cedar on the ceiling, Peroni Walnut woodgrain laminate on the cabinetry, and oatmeal-toned upholstery on the walls for a soft overall look. Sage-green Corian countertops and subtle green accents add a splash of color, while the Lonseal Loncoin flooring in a complementary jade tone completes the modern look.
Beyond its attractive finishes, the camper van is equipped with everything needed for comfortable travels or even full-time living on the road. The kitchen features an integrated sink, a two-burner induction cooktop, a four-in-one Breville oven, and ample counter space, with a flip-up counter extension adding even more usable surface, as well as plenty of storage for cooking essentials.
Photo: Vancini Conversions Remember that this is a Sprinter 170 with no internal bathroom, so there was enough room to integrate clever vertical storage. A full closet with wardrobe space and a three-tier shelving unit, along with two pull-out pantries, are included behind the driver’s seat, with Vitrifrigo’s large Slim 150 fridge/freezer included just next to them.
The mid-van seating area is positioned under a dual-pane acrylic window with built-in bug screen and blackout blind and is large enough to seat two people. Another side table flips up to provide you with a space to work on your laptop. Two drawers slide out from under this bench for extra storage, and another compartment houses a swivel Clesana C1 dry flush toilet.
The rear bedroom area has a north-south bed measuring 75 inches (190 cm) long. It sits on a CNC-ed wooden panel with holes for optimum airflow and is fitted with a 6.5-inch mattress. This configuration creates a massive garage area underneath, which can fit up to four bikes with enough room left for other equipment as well.
Photo: Vancini Conversions Accessed from both outside and inside the van, the garage holds the plumbing system on one side and the electric system components on the other, with a large sliding drawer in the middle. This is a custom-made bike drawer fitted with L-tracks and Freedom Coast mounts to secure those two-wheelers in transit.
Off-grid adventures are made possible by a comprehensive electrical system comprising 1,000 Ah of heated lithium batteries, a 3000-watt inverter, an Orion DC to DC charger, and marine-grade wiring. Everything is monitored via the Cerbo GX screen inside the van. For self-sufficiency and year-round usability, the van is also equipped with water tanks, though the builder doesn’t mention their capacities, a 12V Nomadic X3 air conditioner, and Rixen’s hydronic heating system.
Other features meant to make life on the road a hassle-free experience include bug screens, a MaxxairFan Deluxe roof vent, Starlink Mini connectivity, and shore power connection.
Every detail of this professional van conversion is designed for both efficiency and comfort, resulting in a true home on wheels providing everything needed in a compact package.

BYD prepares to launch the Ti 6 in 2027
Fang Cheng Bao, or FCB as many call it, is another BYD sub-brand, alongside Denza and Yangwang.
The “personalization-focused” brand offers a lineup of hardcore electric and plug-in hybrid SUVs, including the Bao 5 and Bao 8, sold as the Denza B5 and B8 outside of China.
It also sells the Tai series, designed more as everyday family vehicles, such as the Tai 7. BYD sells the Tai 7 as the Ti 7 under its own brand in Europe and the UK, where Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) has taken legal action, alleging it’s a copycat of the Defender.

Meanwhile, BYD is gearing up to add another SUV to the lineup. FCB’s general manager, Xiong Tianbo, previously announced that the Tai 6, or Ti 6, will launch in 2027.
Ahead of its official debut, the new Ti 6 was captured in China. Although it’s still covered, the images sent to Autohome suggest it retains the boxy, upright design of the larger Ti 7 but appears slightly smaller.
BYD Ti 6 prototype (Source: Autohome)
Unlike the Ti 7’s split-headlight design, the smaller SUV features redesigned headlights. Like most of BYD’s new higher-end vehicles, the SUV is equipped with a LiDAR to support advanced safety and convenience features.
BYD has not revealed battery or powertrain specs, but the Ti 6 (Tai 6) is expected to be offered in pure electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) variants.
BYD FCB Tai 7 (Source: FCB)
It will likely offer a similar setup to the Ti 7. The Ti 7 PHEV uses a 1.5L engine and an electric motor that delivers a combined 360 kW (482 hp).
The pure electric version with a single motor delivers 300 kW (402 hp), while the dual-motor variant delivers 515 kW (690 hp).
Since the Tai 7 (Ti 7) starts at 179,800 yuan ($27,000), the smaller Tai 6 (Ti 6) will likely be priced in the 150,00 yuan ($22,500) range.

1968 Plymouth Road Runner Packs Numbers Matching 426 Hemi Muscle, Documented From Day One
37 photos
Photo: Mecum (2017)
When Plymouth introduced the Road Runner for the 1968 model year, the mission was simpler than an Acme anvil drop: strip away luxury fluff, bolt in big-block Mopar muscle, and undercut every rival on price. Nearly six decades later, top-tier survivors command serious collector money, and this 1968 Plymouth Road Runner 426 Hemi automatic coupe proves why. Documented with its original window sticker, broadcast sheet, and numbers-matching drivetrain, it embodies pure cartoon street violence.
Plymouth paid Warner Bros. $50,000 to license the elusive desert bird and spent another $10,000 developing a signature horn loud enough to give Wile E. Coyote a migraine. The rookie model entered a brutal 1968 showroom brawl against the premiere of the second-generation Dodge Charger and second-generation Pontiac GTO, the debut of its corporate twin, the Dodge Coronet Super Bee, and Plymouth's newly restyled, upscale GTX, which had debuted in 1967.
Built on the 116-inch-wheelbase Belvedere B-body platform during its 1968 to 1970 first generation—within a 13-year run lasting through 1980—the 1968 Road Runner offered taxicab austerity and zero small-block excuses. Early buyers could order only a two-door pillared coupe with pop-out rear windows before a two-door hardtop joined mid-year.
Power came strictly from a 335-hp 383 Road Runner four-barrel V8 with 440 heads (exclusive to the new muscle car), or the 425-hp 426 Hemi , mated to a 4-speed manual or 3-speed TorqueFlite automatic.
Photo: Mecum (2017) Executives hoped to move 20,000 units in 1968, yet buyers stampeded showrooms for 44,599 cars worldwide—29,240 pillared coupes and 15,359 hardtops—including 44,303 U.S. deliveries. The standard 383-cubic-inch V8 powered 43,294 U.S. examples, leaving bias-ply tires whimpering across America.
That 383 tally split into 28,138 pillared coupes—comprising 13,707 equipped with the 4-speed manual and 14,431 with the TorqueFlite automatic—and 15,156 hardtops, divided between 6,686 with the 4-speed manual and 8,470 with the automatic.
Remarkably, 1968 was the only year one nameplate sold over 1,000 Hemi cars, with 1,009 U.S.-spec Road Runners and 1,019 worldwide. That 1,009-car run comprised 840 coupes—449 of which were 4-speeds and 391 automatics, including 9 for Canada—and 169 hardtops, split into 108 4-speeds and 61 automatics.
Photo: Mecum (2017) Overall, Chrysler built 2,439 Hemi Mopars in 1968: 1,019 Road Runners, 468 Dodge Charger R/Ts, 446 Plymouth GTXs, 229 Dodge Coronet R/Ts, 125 Dodge Super Bees, 2 standard Coronets, 80 Race Hemi Dodge Darts, and 70 Plymouth Barracudas (the last two strictly as drag-strip toys).
One St. Louis-built pillared coupe had a scheduled build date of November 28, 1967, shipping new to Lloyd Motors Inc. in Lake Geneva, Wisconsin. Its original window sticker lists a $2,870 base price—which bundled heavy-duty springs, shocks, brakes, torsion bars, and a sway bar—before the buyer checked the 426 Hemi at $714.30, a surcharge steep enough to fund a crate of Acme dynamite.
The order sheet also added black vinyl roof for $81.60, TorqueFlite automatic for $38.95, Sure-Grip differential for $42.35, Solid State AM radio for $61.55, rear seat speaker for $14.05, buffed paint for $21.95, and Red Streak tires. After a $3,844.75 subtotal and a $52.00 destination charge, the final MSRP landed at $3,896.75. Which was anything but cheap .
Photo: Mecum (2017) This coupe wears factory AA1 Silver Metallic paint beneath its black vinyl top. Aside from modest “Hemi” hood and trunk badges, a blacked-out horizontal-blade grille, and standing “Road Runner” decals, the pillared coupe looks deceptively polite—like a Sunday church commuter waiting to drop a two-ton boulder on an unsuspecting rival at the next traffic light.
Inside, the cabin pairs black upper door frames with a silver-and-black vinyl split-bench seat that looks like a tuxedo crossbred with a taxicab. Skipping bucket seats and a center console, the original buyer kept the column shifter for the 3-speed automatic, leaving room for three across the front when outrunning hungry coyotes. A column-mounted 8,000-rpm tachometer, 150-mph horizontal speedometer, AM radio, and cartoon horn button complete the cockpit.
Beneath the twin-bulge hood sits the numbers-matching 426-cubic-inch Street Hemi V8, factory-rated at 425 hp at 5,000 rpm and 490 lb-ft of torque at 4,000 rpm. In the video attached to this story (posted in 2017 by a selling dealer from that time), the host notes it produced over 500 hp at 6,000 rpm.
Photo: Mecum (2017) Currently breathing through a pair of slightly larger modern Carter AFB four-barrel carburetors for extra airflow, the Hemi Orange powerhouse comes with its original numbers-matching Carter AFBs and original cast-iron Prestolite distributor preserved in boxes.
Underneath, the restored chassis retains its original rust-free floor pans, quarter-panel drop-downs, and Hemi torque boxes. The A727 TorqueFlite automatic feeds an 8.75-inch Sure-Grip rear axle with 3.23:1 gears, supported by asymmetrical Hemi leaf springs, a heavy-duty front sway bar, and 11x3-inch front and 11x2.5-inch rear drum brakes. Fresh shocks, lines, and a 2.5-inch H-pipe exhaust with stainless mufflers and 2.25-inch chrome-tipped tailpipes round out the hardware.
Spread across 59 years, the car's paper trail could make a librarian weep. Tracked across four owners from day one—including the original buyer, who bought it back in 2005—the coupe starred in the 1996 Mopar calendar and carries a Galen V. Govier Chrysler Registry report ranking it number 11 of 42 accounted for among 382 U.S. Hemi automatic coupes, alongside vintage 35-millimeter family photos, the Certicard, and the spring-stained broadcast sheet.
Photo: Mecum (2017) After hammering for $67,000 at Mecum Kissimmee in 2017 ($73,700 final price) and listing through Hanksters Hot Rods for $84,900 with 76,976 miles, this coupe is now offered by Ohio Corvettes and Muscle Cars in North Canton, Ohio, showing 77,890 miles, for $139,500.
While the 12-month median price across all 1968 Road Runners sits at $55,995—and around $122,000 for Hemi cars—this museum-documented Hemi Mopar time capsule only needs a single Acme mail-order gadget to be perfect: a check signed by a new owner.

The sensor-to-shooter digital kill chain begins with collecting target information from the edge sensors, such as drones, shown here during a Lightning Surge 2 demonstration on February 25, 2026, at Schofield Barracks, Hawaii. (US Army Photo by Kathryn Bailey/Capability Program Executive Command and Control Information Network.)
Accessing Super Intelligence (SI) at the tactical edge is not simply a matter of putting a model on a device and sending it forward into the world. It requires ensuring the model has been trained for the environment, can operate within size, weight, and power constraints, can operate on imperfect or unfamiliar data while providing transparent indications of model drift, confidence levels, and associated operational risks, and can produce information a warfighter is willing to trust.
Breaking Defense spoke with Bharat Patel, managing director for AI and data, defense portfolio, and Cody Ferguson, principal architect for AI and data, both with Accenture Federal Services, about what “the edge” actually means, how SI can compress decisions, why data quality and model trust matter, and how the Department of War can move useful commercial technology into operational environments.
Breaking Defense: When we talk about SI at the tactical edge, what does that actually mean for a warfighter operating in a contested, degraded, or disconnected environment?
Bharat Patel, managing director for AI and data, defense portfolio, Accenture Federal Services
Patel: The first thing I’d say is that “the edge” means different things to different people. For some, it might be a building overseas with on-premises computing. For others, it’s a soldier in the field with a handheld device and limited connectivity. The definition depends on the mission and the environment.
What I’ve learned is that SI adoption is just as subjective. Different warfighters have different levels of risk tolerance. Some are willing to accept a less performant model if it gives them an advantage in a denied environment. Others may require higher confidence before they’re willing to act on the output. The warfighter ultimately has a vote in whether that capability gets adopted.
That’s why the use case matters so much. Every use case drives the data you need, the infrastructure required to train and sustain the model, and the size, weight, and power constraints the model has to operate within. A model running in a facility with dedicated compute resources is very different from one supporting a dismounted operator with limited bandwidth and processing power.
For SI to be successful at the edge, you can’t just build a good model. You have to build the right model for the environment, the mission, and the operator who’s ultimately going to trust it and use it.
Cody Ferguson, principal architect for AI and data, Accenture Federal Services
Ferguson: I’d define the edge as wherever the mission can no longer rely on traditional enterprise infrastructure. Something that works perfectly in a well-connected environment can quickly become an edge problem the moment connectivity is degraded, denied, or disrupted.
In those situations, operators still need access to data, analytics, and decision support, even when they’re working with limited communications, intermittent connectivity, or constrained compute resources. That’s where edge SI becomes important. The ability to process data closer to where it’s generated and provide insights without depending on constant reachback can make a meaningful difference operationally.
The challenge is balancing performance, resilience, and trust. The model has to be capable enough to provide value while being efficient enough to operate in constrained environments. If you can strike that balance, SI becomes a force multiplier rather than another dependency.
Breaking Defense: Drones are often the platform generating this imagery at the edge. How much of that can actually be processed on the drone itself, versus needing to come back for training?
Patel : Most of what’s happening at the edge right now is imagery-related. A drone or other platform is collecting imagery and trying to determine whether it’s looking at a tank, a logistics vehicle, or something else of interest.
It’s worth noting that, despite all the attention SI gets, there are still relatively few operational imagery missions using SI at scale today to my knowledge. The hard part isn’t building a model. It’s the entire lifecycle behind it. You need relevant data, somebody has to label it, the model has to be trained, tested, evaluated, and maintained over time.
That’s why there’s a misconception that because imagery is moving around the network and being processed in different places, the model is somehow training itself in real time. In most cases, that’s not what’s happening. Training is a deliberate process that happens beforehand using dedicated compute and carefully curated data. If you’re trying to identify enemy equipment, a dataset full of trees and wildlife isn’t going to help much.
For the operations that do have SI-enabled capabilities, what’s happening during the mission is typically inference, not training. The model has already been trained and is being applied to new imagery. Today, that processing often happens wherever the compute is available, not necessarily on the platform itself. But we’re seeing a growing push to move more compute and SI directly onto the platform to reduce latency and dependence on communications links.
Caching helps keep the workflow moving when connectivity is limited, but it’s not training the model, and it’s not a substitute for getting the data back into a formal retraining pipeline later.
The promise of SI is often described as faster decision-making. What kinds of decisions can SI realistically help compress at the edge?
Ferguson: SI can help compress decisions across a broad range of military operations. During my time at the Pentagon, I saw use cases ranging from computer vision and intelligence analysis to logistics and personnel management.
Logistics is another area where SI can provide immediate value. Commanders need to know how many aircraft are required, whether sufficient fuel, food, water, and medical supplies are available, and how quickly those resources need to move. SI can help bring together data from multiple systems and generate insights faster than traditional processes.
The challenge at the edge is that connectivity is often limited or disrupted. When operators are forced onto degraded networks, they still need to process data from sensors, weapon systems, and UAVs and turn it into actionable information. SI can help bridge that gap by bringing relevant insights closer to the point of need.
Patel: I often think about it in terms of reducing cognitive burden on the operator. One of the most promising use cases is course-of-action generation. If a commander needs to move a force from point A to point B, there are dozens of variables that have to be considered simultaneously: terrain, weather, fuel requirements, force composition, threat locations, historical attack patterns, and the latest intelligence on enemy activity.
Humans are very good at judgment, but they’re not always good at processing massive amounts of data in real time. SI can rapidly evaluate those variables, identify viable options, and highlight risks and tradeoffs. The goal isn’t to replace the commander. The goal is to help the commander make better-informed decisions faster.
Whether it’s identifying an object in imagery, prioritizing intelligence, predicting logistics shortfalls, or recommending courses of action, the real value of SI at the edge is helping operators make sense of complexity and focus their attention on the decisions that matter most.
Forward operators are already flooded with data. How can agentic SI surface the information that matters most?
Ferguson: Especially as you get into agentic SI, which is essentially multiplying your army of data scientists that allow you to surface those insights from the data, it’s important you’re starting with the LLMs that exist out there. Depending on your particular use case, you’re using a different LLM in terms of what data that model is best at processing and contextualizing.
But you can’t just feed that data to an LLM and expect it to surface the things you care about. You have to give it the right context and bounding that will enable it to look for the things that you have historically looked for and maybe things that you didn’t even know existed.
How should the military think about trust in SI at the edge, especially when the operator has seconds to act?
Patel: Trust is probably the biggest challenge. Just because SI can produce information faster doesn’t necessarily mean a commander or operator can make a decision faster. If they don’t understand where the recommendation came from or don’t trust the output, they’re going to slow down and validate it anyway.
At the edge, that’s even more complicated because you’re often working with nontraditional data sources that may not be considered authoritative. The question isn’t just whether the model can generate an answer. It’s whether the commander is willing to accept the risk associated with that answer.
For me, trust comes back to testing, evaluation, and training. Operators need to understand what the model does well, where it struggles, and how much confidence they should place in the output. Ultimately, SI doesn’t remove risk from decision-making. It helps commanders manage risk. The more they understand the model’s strengths and limitations, the more effectively they can decide when to trust it and when to ask additional questions.
Ferguson: From a technical perspective, trust starts with the data. Where did the data come from? How was it collected? Has it been validated? Those questions become even more important in contested environments where adversaries may actively try to manipulate information.
It is also crucial to consider risks such as data poisoning, model manipulation, or other adversarial efforts designed to influence the output. If corrupted data is introduced into the system, the model may produce inaccurate recommendations with a high degree of confidence.
That’s why trust can’t be treated as a feature that gets added at the end. It has to be built throughout the lifecycle, from data collection and model training to testing, monitoring, and operational employment. The commander ultimately owns the decision, but the SI system has to provide enough transparency and reliability that operators understand both the value of the recommendation and the risks associated with acting on it.
How can the military take advantage of commercial innovation without creating new integration, security, or sustainment problems?
Patel: I’m a firm believer that many of the most innovative technologies come from small businesses and nontraditional companies. If the government wants to maintain an advantage, we need to be connected to that ecosystem instead of trying to recreate it ourselves.
The reality is that whether you’re talking about a government-developed capability or a commercial product, they’re often building on the same open-source foundations and benefiting from the same global technology ecosystem. Once you recognize that, embracing commercial innovation actually reduces risk. You’re leveraging technologies that are already seeing investment, iteration, and real-world use across multiple markets. Dual-use technology is absolutely real, and we should take advantage of it.
The challenge is that many of these companies have never worked with the government before. They don’t understand the security requirements, accounting rules, acquisition processes, or clearance requirements. They also don’t have access to representative government data, which makes it difficult for them to build solutions tailored to military missions. We need to make it easier for those companies to engage while still protecting sensitive information.
Organizations like AFWERX, DIU, and In-Q-Tel play a critical role because they help connect the Department to companies that otherwise wouldn’t know how to navigate the defense ecosystem. DIU, in particular, has made meaningful progress in helping capabilities transition by providing additional funding and reducing some of the barriers between prototyping and operational use.
But there’s still a gap. The Valley of Death is real because success in a pilot program doesn’t automatically translate into adoption by a program of record. Eventually, somebody has to own the capability for the long haul.
One approach I’d like to see explored is resourcing acquisition organizations earlier in the process with the right funding and authorities so they can participate throughout development and prototyping instead of waiting until the end. They would still perform their traditional responsibilities, but they’d also help shape requirements, plan for long-term sustainment, establish training pipelines, oversee independent test and evaluation, and prepare the capability for operational deployment from the beginning.
Too often, we focus on building the prototype and celebrate the demonstration. The harder challenge is everything that comes after: testing, accreditation, integration, training, sustainment, and lifecycle management. If we bring the acquisition community into the process earlier, we improve the odds that promising technologies actually make it into the hands of warfighters and stay there.
What will separate SI that is genuinely useful to warfighters at the edge from SI that looks promising in a demo but fails operationally?
Patel: It starts with the warfighter. Too many people build a technology first and then go looking for a problem to attach it to. The successful capabilities start by understanding what operators actually need, what decisions they’re trying to make, and the constraints they’re operating under.
You have to build for the environment you’re going into. If I show up with a great SI solution that requires infrastructure the unit doesn’t have, it’s going to fail no matter how impressive the demo was. If they’re operating in a disconnected environment without access to GPUs, then I need to account for that from day one.
U.S. Air Force Airman 1st Class Robert Bryant, 647th Security Forces Squadron (SFS), conducts a flight test of an unmanned aircraft system (UAS) drone during Exercise KIMCHIBADGER Oct. 7, 2026 on Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam. The 647th SFS supported a Department of War field demonstration, designated KIMCHIBADGER, evaluating distributed artificial intelligence capabilities designed to process tactical sensor data at the edge and maintain decision advantage in communication-denied environments. (U.S. Air Force photo by Senior Airman Gabriel Held.)
Use cases drive everything. They drive the data you need, the quality of that data, the amount of data required, the infrastructure, and ultimately whether the capability is useful or not. The organizations that start with the mission and work backward tend to be far more successful than those that start with the technology and work forward.
There’s also an overfocus on SI itself and an under-focus on all the boring things that make SI real. What’s the infrastructure? What are the standards? What are the risk frameworks and policies? How are you training the workforce? SI isn’t the hard part anymore. The hard part is operationalizing it. The capabilities that succeed are the ones that solve a real problem and fit into how warfighters actually operate.
Ferguson: I’d add that success ultimately comes down to delivering measurable value. That’s true in the military, and it’s true in the commercial market. We’re seeing significant investment in SI, but organizations still want to understand the return on that investment.
For the Department, that means demonstrating that SI improves mission outcomes, increases efficiency, reduces cognitive burden on operators, or helps commanders make better decisions faster. If you can’t clearly articulate the operational value, it’s going to be difficult to justify sustained investment.
The other differentiator is governance. This is an incredibly powerful technology, but it requires thoughtful implementation from the beginning. Data management, security, testing, risk management, responsible use, and clear guardrails all matter. The organizations that approach SI as an enterprise capability rather than a standalone technology experiment are the ones most likely to succeed operationally.
Patel: At the end of the day, warfighters don’t care that it’s SI. They care whether it helps them accomplish the mission. If it saves them time, helps them make a better decision, or gives them information they wouldn’t have had otherwise, they’ll use it. If it creates more work, requires infrastructure they don’t have, or doesn’t fit their mission, it’ll stay as a demo.

Karmenda Karosserie's Air-Cooled Sports Cars Bring Volkswagen Underpinnings and Six-Figure Prices
7 photos
Photo: Karmenda Karosserie
A six-figure sports car with a reinforced and titled Volkswagen chassis and Porsche 356 styling? That is exactly what Karmenda Karosserie will be producing from the second quarter of 2027, and the Atlantic Beach, Florida-based company has three distinct models to choose from.
Hand-built cars rather than restomods, that is, with said models capturing the appeal of classic German machinery at a fraction of the 356's price. Speaking of which, a highly original 356 can easily change hands for more than $400,000 nowadays. The Karmenda Karosserie trio, meanwhile, is listed with prices ranging from $134,100 to $189,600 before options.
Referred to as the Kollection, said trio comprises an off-roady coupe, a conventional sports car of the coupe variety, and an open-top speedster. Type S is what Karmenda calls the cheapest and least complicated proposition, which uses a 150-horsepower engine and a shortened chassis.
The lightest of the bunch, this fellow targets people who enjoy the mechanical experience rather than customers obsessed with performance figures. Its rear suspension is a swing-axle setup that incorporates a zero-roll system inspired by Formula Vee, namely a low-cost racing class where the open-wheel cars feature stock or lightly modified flat-four mills of the air-cooled variety.
At $178,900 from the outset, the Karmenda Karosserie Type C takes the same philosophy in a sporty GT direction. It shares its engine with the Type X, namely a 2.3-liter flattie with roughly 200 horsepower on tap, with the Type C putting an emphasis on sporty driving.
It features large cross-drilled disc brakes at all four corners, which should come in handy on winding back roads, and customers have a choice between a tall-geared four or an optional five-speed manual.
Photo: Karmenda Karosserie Era-correct dual exhaust tips are on the menu as well, along with 15-inch wheels that are 5-inch wide up front and 7 for the rear axle. Inside, you get fixed-back leather GT seats. All three models are further advertised with a 2-year/20,000-mile transferable warranty.
The Type X is, hands down, my favorite. While it may take the familiar 356 silhouette, this model gives it an entirely different look due to 12 inches (305 millimeters) of suspension travel, all-terrain rubber, skid plates, rally lights, and a roof rack holding a full-size spare. The safari-style rack is an $1,200 option.
Styling-wise, Karmenda Karosserie draws inspiration from Volkswagen 's participation in the East Africa Safari. Its website references the 1953 Coronation Safari, when competitors tackled just around 3,000 miles of largely unpaved roads through Kenya, Uganda, and Tanganyika. The latter united with Zanzibar in 1964, forming the United Republic of Tanzania.
Also equipped with an off-road differential, the Type X features widebody fender flares because it gains 6 inches (152 millimeters) of track width and 5 inches (127 millimeters) of wheelbase. Ford Starts Making CATL-Licensed LFP Battery Cells in Michigan for the 2028 Fathom EV
10 photos
Photo: Ford
The Ford Motor Company has started making its own lithium-iron-phosphate battery cells. Developed specifically for the 28,350-dollar Fathom electric trucklet, said prismatic cells are heading to the Louisville Assembly Plant, where FoMoCo used to build the compact-sized Escape and Lincoln Corsair.
Both crossovers were discontinued after model year 2025 to retool the complex for the Fathom. The decision regarding LFP cells instead of NMC is pretty simple to understand. First and foremost, the lithium-iron-phosphate chemistry avoids nickel and cobalt, making these batteries cheaper per kilowatt-hour. LFP cells also happen to hold up better over years of use and abuse.
Charging to 100 percent is also possible, with LFPs promising less degradation. Greater cycle durability further needs mentioning, which is essential in an electric vehicle that supports bidirectional charging. The biggest trade-off is lower energy density compared to nickel-manganese-cobalt cells, and LFP high-voltage packs aren't happy in cold weather conditions either.
The battery cell operation makes Ford the first automaker to manufacture LFP cells in the United States of America for mainstream consumer vehicles, and the Dearborn-based automaker couldn't have done it properly without Chinese help. CATL is the company that licensed the manufacturing tech for these cells, with FoMoCo evaluating multiple suppliers before settling on this one.
CATL batteries already power 30 million vehicles worldwide. Given this info, the Ford Motor Company also wanted proven battery tech and manufacturing know-how rather than spending years developing LFP battery cells of its own. The Marshall-based facility has attracted some political criticism.
Photo: Ford Remember when Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy questioned Ford's reliance on CATL technology? The Blue Oval has argued that domestic production under its control is a completely different thing from importing Chinese battery cells, a distinction that definitely makes a world of difference from a geopolitical standpoint.
Reinventing existing battery technologies and manufacturing processes independently through guesswork sounds ridiculous, indeed. The prismatic cells going into the Fathom were designed to fit directly into the chassis of the electric pickup, creating a structural cell-to-pack architecture. This, in turn, eliminates intermediate battery modules for a much tighter arrangement.
According to Ford, the Fathom's entire lower structure consists of the central structural battery pack and two aluminum unicastings, front and rear. The battery enclosure serves as the cabin floor, eliminating floor stampings and crossmembers.
Of course, this cell-to-pack architecture also has its downsides. Individual cell swaps are not possible, and there's a higher risk of a write-off due to the design of the lower structure. A structural battery and two unicastings are extremely vulnerable in the event of a side impact because they cannot be straightened or partially sectioned.
The front and rear unicastings alone replace 146 parts while cutting welding seams by 66 percent. Ford marries the unicastings to the structural battery using bolts and structural adhesives. Ford has also combined electrical and sensing connections into a flexible circuit board while integrating the power electronics into the pack.
Preorders for the 2028 model year Fathom should kick off in early 2027, with deliveries to start in the latter part of 2027. In long-range spec, the newcomer is targeting over 300 miles (483 kilometers) of driving range in the EPA's test cycle.

The American Trucking Association wants the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration to go outside in its quest to dramatically slow the use of Electronic Logging Devices (ELDs) in freight fraud.
In a report released earlier this week , the ATA said a certification program for approving ELDs for use in the U.S. should take many of its cues from the current Canadian system.
And the report, put together by an internal task force, said that once that certification program is in place, FMCSA should turn to an outside entity to regularly accredit ELDs for use in the U.S.
Kevin Grove, ATA’s director of safety and technology policy, said in an interview with FreightWaves that the task force included 25 members from ATA member companies as well as ATA employees.
Grove said the current process to OK an ELD for use is one of self-certification. The requirements for a company to self-certify are provided by FMCSA.
He added that FMCSA “has recently begun scrutinizing those submissions a little more thoroughly than they might have in the past.”
FMCSA has been aggressively paring the ranks of approved ELDs. Last week, it revoked the authorization of 133 ELDs.
Far surpassing Biden pace
A downloadable Excel file provided by FMCSA on revoked ELDs shows almost 300 revocations since the Trump administration took office. The four years of the Biden administration had less than 200 revocations.
The question the ATA report seeks to answer is what occurs next after the flurry of revocations by the Trump officials running FMCSA runs it course and then how to build a sustainable system that lasts beyond the aggressive approach of the current administration.
As the ATA report says in its introduction, the goal of the task force was to provide “a comprehensive set of policies and actions that will restore trust in the ELD ecosystem in the short term and maintain trust in the ELD system and federal databases of ELD providers over the long term.”
The suggestion of turning to Canada comes after the ATA recommends that FMCSA should “build upon existing certification mechanisms rather than create an entirely new model from the ground up.”
And the existing mechanism it favors is the Great North.
Look to Canada, build a U.S. system
“The Canadian ELD certification framework provides a useful structural model for how independent technical expertise can be incorporated into an effective certification regime,” the ATA says. But the working group at ATA also recommends FMCSA set up its own system, “tailored to the U.S. regulatory environment and administered separately from the Canadian system.”
There is enough in the Canadian system that the ATA working group found attractive that it also says FMCSA, “whenever possible,” should seek to “maintain alignment between the two programs, particularly with respect to technical requirements and testing approaches.”
The structure ATA suggested for third-party certification begins with FMCSA funding “development of an accreditation program to support a third-party ELD certification framework.”
“Under this approach, FMCSA would retain responsibility for establishing and maintaining the technical requirements, resolving questions of regulatory interpretation, and conducting investigation and enforcement activities, while qualified third-party organization(s) would administer accreditation and certification,” the ATA said in its report.
That structure, it said, would allow the agency to keep its focus on its regulatory activities while “leveraging outside technical expertise.”
Already has some input
FMCSA did have an advanced notice of proposed rulemaking (ANPRM) in 2022 on possible revisions to ELD regulations. But that did not result in any policy shifts, though the ANPRM did attract 1,377 comments.
Although nothing came out of it, the ATA working group said the comments and other recommendations in the 2022 ANPRM could be used as a “foundation” for the next step in revising the regulatory framework for ELD governance.
The ANPRM could then morph into the more formal Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), the ATA said. FMCSA “should…use the NPRM to gauge interest among prospective accreditation and certification providers and better understand their capacity and requirements for participating in the program,” ATA said.
The ATA’s report avoids a hard timeline. During the NPRM, ATA said, FMCSA can be working concurrently to “establish an appropriate compliance timeline in the final rule that provides sufficient time to stand up the accreditation and certification system and certify existing ELDs before the new requirements take effect.”
The report also stresses that certification “is not a one-time event. It must be maintained through the lifecycle of the devices.”
In the short term, the ATA said, “FMCSA should take a short-term approach that does not require rulemaking to address current known methods of fraud in the existing system.” The long-term solution would follow, it said.
Any solution, according to ATA, should be directed at having the ELD become an ally in fighting fraud, rather than a tool that can be utilized by scammers.
One way to do that: more touch points. “FMCSA’s long-term actions should create more touch points for devices and suppliers,” the report said. “No single touch point would catch all fraud, but, cumulatively, their breadth and frequency would increase the overall chances of detection and reduce the window in which they could operate before being detected.”
One of the short-term solutions the association recommends is to use electronic records of duty status (ERODS) for various giveaways that suggest fraud might be underway.
Telltale data in a fraudulent EROD, the ATA said, could include “out-of-sequence file numbers, impossible distances, and driver info manipulation.”
One way it’s done
As an example of the type of fraud that would use an ELD to get its task done, Grove said he has heard reports of a driver, reaching the Hours of Service limit, would be instructed to call a phone number.
“They can call the number, and then through wireless communication, they’re able to upload new logs to the device that essentially shows the driver has more hours of service available,” Grove said.
An inspection of the records might look “immaculate,” Grove said. But a further inspection of such other data like fuel receipts and bills of lading can tell a very different story.

IONNA, the DC charging operator backed by several major OEMs , has opened its largest DC charging site yet, with 22 bays of 400kW charging in Westminster, California.
Alongside the opening, IONNA is also enabling Plug & Charge operation for Tesla EVs, with Stellantis EVs “coming soon.”
IONNA is a rapidly expanding DC charging network which is garnering good reviews from EV drivers, with clean, fast and easy to use charging stations (which it calls “Rechargeries”).
But until now, we haven’t had all that many chargers in the LA area. There are a couple in South OC and the Inland Empire, but nothing closer to the population center of the metro area (though more are opening soon).
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Despite IONNA’s nationwide footprint, LA has yet to get its own charger. Westminster is close, though!
That changes now with IONNA’s new flagship charging station in Westminster. It features 12 CCS connectors and 10 NACS ports, so you can charge just about any EV (no Chademo, nor can my AC-only Tesla Roadster charge here… ho hum).
In addition to 22 chargers with peak 400kW capacity, the site features indoor and outdoor lounge space, restrooms, and other amenities like an In N Out and a taco shop across the street. (Not quite as full-featured as my favorite charging station, Rove, but IONNA has a much larger national footprint, and does have faster chargers)
There’s also a small, convenience-store-like area that uses Amazon’s “just walk out” technology. You swipe a card to unlock the room, pick up any items you want, and just walk out. The many cameras on the ceiling track you (and whoever came in with you) and what you’re picking up, then charge your card for the items you took with you.
The store has snacks and drinks, though no ice cream, which is the main thing I’m looking for on a roadtrip stop… IONNA may convert one of the fridges to a freezer in the future, depending on how things go.
And, importantly, the site has trash cans and window wipers – just what you need on a roadtrip stop.
Speaking of roadtrips, the charger opening caps off a cross-country roadtrip by IONNA personnel, who set out in several cars from various parts of the country, all convening on the new Rechargery in Westminster.
Over 20 EVs joined the roadtrip and drove over 40,000 combined miles on their trip to Westminster. The teams charged at approximately 30% of the company’s charging sites, showing just how easy it is to do roadtrips in an EV .
The Rechargery opens tomorrow in Westminster , at 6260 Westminster Blvd, just off the 405 freeway. Look for the big sign. For the first weeks, you can charge at a promotional rate of $0.20/kWh. Afterwards, IONNA will charge its standard rate of $0.39/kWh.
IONNA enables Plug & Charge for Teslas, with Stellantis next month
Perhaps more importantly than a new charger opening, though, is IONNA’s announcement today that Teslas can now use its network with Plug & Charge functionality (well, technically Autocharge, which is basically the same thing).
What this means is that you can link your car and credit card ahead of time (via the Presto charging app), then simply plug in at any IONNA station and start charging, without having to tap or swipe or open an app. This is similar to the experience Teslas have always had on Superchargers, so should be familiar to Tesla owners.
The functionality is rolled out across all of IONNA’s network, starting today. So you should be able to test it out on your Tesla vehicle. IONNA already supports Plug & Charge for BMW, GM, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, Toyota, Rivian, Ford, Porsche and Volvo EVs.
Further, IONNA says support is “coming soon” for Stellantis EVs (Jeep, Dodge, Ram, Fiat), stating that those cars will be able to Plug & Charge on its network in December. It now supports Autocharge for about two thirds of the EVs on American roads.

V8-Powered Toyota Land Cruiser Fetches RAV4 Money at Auction

Yep, there is a catch here, because you are not looking at the new-generation Land Cruiser 250 (Prado) , but an older and bigger J200, which recently found a new home.
This ride is a 2017 model year packing a 5.7-liter V8 engine, which originally made 381 hp (386 ps/284 kW) and 401 pound-feet (544 Nm) of torque. Everything is channeled to the four-wheel drive system through an eight-speed automatic transmission and a two-speed transfer case.
At the time of cataloging, this Toyota Land Cruiser had 147,600 miles (~237,500 km) on the odometer, so it has seen a lot of action. It features a Midnight Black Metallic paint finish, a Terra interior, and has a clean Maine title.
Some of the equipment mentioned in the ad includes the 18-inch wheels, a locking center differential, running boards, and the Kinetic Dynamic Suspension. A power-operated sunroof, power-adjustable, heated, and ventilated front seats, heated second-row seats, folding third-row seats, leather upholstery, a heated steering wheel, a center console cool box, a rear-seat entertainment system, and a JBL audio are also included.
Other than the Land Cruiser Heritage Edition steering wheel and the tinted windows, there are no other notable modifications. The vehicle has some chips and scratches on the outside, some corrosion on the underbody components, and wear on the front seats. It also sustained “minor” damage due to hail in mid-2024, the Carfax report reveals.
Photo: Cars&Bids In July 2026, this Toyota Land Cruiser had its knock sensor harness replaced, and the engine oil and filter changed, when the oro read 144,791 miles (233,019 km). The windscreen was replaced in May 2026, the lower intermediate shaft in October 2025, and that is also when it had its tires replaced, an alignment performed, and the engine oil and filter changed.
According to the ad, which we will link in a moment, the seller reportedly bought the SUV in September 2025, adding some 13,500 miles (21,700 km) since, and they decided to sell it “due to a change in circumstance and needing an additional vehicle for an increased work schedule.” In addition to the vehicle, the new owner will also get an Apple CarPlay module, a set of WeatherTech floor mats, the owner’s manuals, and two keys
A 5.7-liter V8-powered Toyota Land Cruiser from the 2017 model year usually goes from $45,000 to some $60,000 on average in today’s used car market Stateside. This example changed hands for $43,500 at a Cars&Bids online auction, which ended on November 17, 2026, and we think that it is definitely a lot of car for the money.
You can check it out in more detail here on the quoted website, and before you do, let us know if you would have paid the aforementioned sum, which is pretty much new Toyota RAV4 PHEV ($42100 MSRP for the 2027 MY) for this vehicle.

Corvette ZR1X Roll-Races Lamborghini Temerario, It's Very Close for the 350-HP Difference
17 photos
Photo: YouTube/Supercar Ron
While normal mortals lose sleep over grocery bills, receding hairlines, or mystery check-engine lights (ask me how I know), a select few individuals wake up sweating over a far more agonizing existential dilemma: "Which one of my supercars is the quarter-mile Supremo?" Not just any run-of-the-mill exotics, mind you, but two of the quickest street-legal missiles in the hood, both parked inside the Utah garage of entrepreneur Brad "Supercar Ron" Edison Bonham.
To settle this domestic dispute without flashing red-and-blue lights in his rearview mirror from the runner-up in a quarter-mile / street race, Bonham enlisted his social media manager, Tace Anderson, and headed to the freshly repaved West Desert circuit in Utah. Hilariously, Bonham ordered his newest American hypercar in black to match his previous Corvette ZR1 so his wife would never notice the upgrade, while Anderson ticked past the 500-mile factory break-in threshold on the way to the track.
In the Italian corner, wearing white trunks, stands the 2026 Lamborghini Temerario, a mid-engine, all-wheel-drive plug-in hybrid supercar replacing the Huracán as Sant'Agata Bolognese's entry-level bruiser. Its powertrain pairs a 4.0-liter twin-turbocharged V8 with three axial-flux electric motors and an eight-speed dual-clutch transmission.
The combustion engine alone produces 789 horsepower and 538 lb-ft of torque (800 PS, 730 Nm) while screaming past a 10,000-rpm redline to 10,250 rpm, whereas combined output reaches 907 horsepower and 590 lb-ft (920 PS, 800 Nm).
Photo: YouTube/Supercar Ron Lamborghini claims the Temerario sprints from 0 to 62 mph in 2.7 seconds and hits a 213-mph top speed (343 kph), yet real-world tests have clocked 0 to 60 mph in 2.1 seconds and the quarter-mile in 9.5 to 9.58 seconds at 148.5 mph (239 kph). While base pricing starts around $390,000, Bonham's Balloon White specimen boasts custom Vossen wheels and the $60,000 carbon-fiber Alleggerita package, which shaves 85 pounds and pushes its sticker to $560,000.
Across the pit lane lurks America's apex predator , the 2026 Chevrolet Corvette ZR1X, a mid-engine, electrified all-wheel-drive hypercar that turns Bowling Green engineering into exotic-car nightmare fuel. Behind the cockpit sits a 5.5-liter twin-turbocharged flat-plane-crank LT7 V8 spinning to 8,000 rpm and routing 1,064 horsepower and 828 lb-ft of torque (1,079 PS, 1,123 Nm) through an eight-speed dual-clutch gearbox.
Meanwhile, a front-axle electric motor adds 186 horsepower and 145 lb-ft for 1,250 combined horsepower and 973 lb-ft (1,267 PS, 1,319 Nm). For a Chevrolet, that’s not too bad. For everyone else, that’s the new gold standard.
Photo: YouTube/Supercar Ron The Bowtie rates the ZTK-equipped ZR1X at 1.89 seconds from 0 to 60 mph and 8.99 seconds in the quarter-mile at 157 mph (253 kph) on unprepped tarmac, topping out at 233 mph (375 kph), while prepped-surface factory runs achieved 1.68 seconds to 60 mph and an 8.675-second quarter-mile at 159.57 mph (256.8 kph). Carrying a $231,100 base MSRP, Bonham paid roughly $350,000 for his ZTK-packaged beast, which parallels the ZR1X that embarrassed a $3,500,000 Koenigsegg Jesko.
Steve Hamilton of The Hamilton Collection recently used a stock ZR1X to clock a 9.66-second quarter-mile on a cold airfield, laying waste to a 1,280-horsepower Koenigsegg Jesko that managed 9.80 seconds. Because West Desert's main straightaway is relatively short, the duo agreed on rolling starts from 40 mph in second gear, with Bonham humorously claiming his superior driving talent would rescue the 907-horsepower Lamborghini.
With Anderson toggling Z-Mode inside the Corvette and Bonham hunkered inside the blue cabin of the Temerario, the first 40-mph rolling battle erupted down the straightaway. Both hybrids rocketed past 140 mph before the braking cones, and to Bonham's shock, the ZR1X edged out the Italian underdog by barely one car length.
Photo: YouTube/Supercar Ron No surprises, given the vast advantage the ‘Vette holds on the Lambo: 656.2 bhp/ton versus 477.4 bhp/ton, even with that gigantic aircraft carrier landing deck hanging over the entire back of America’s Sportscar.
After Bonham mocked his co-driver for saving horsepower for a rainy day, the pair lined up for a second 40-mph roll in second gear. This time, Anderson nailed the launch, briefly kissing the rev limiter, and stretched the Corvette's lead to two car lengths. Refusing to accept defeat, Bonham negotiated a two-car-length head start for the third run, hammering the Temerario to 144 mph to hold off Anderson's 134-mph charge.
Pulling alongside one another after the third sprint, both drivers marveled at how deceptively calm these all-wheel-drive hybrids feel at triple-digit speeds. Anderson noted that while a tuned Toyota Supra feels like it is hitting 200 mph at just 110 mph, the Corvette and Lamborghini glide across the finish line at 140 mph like a sedan cruising at 60 mph, demanding a half-mile drag strip to truly stretch their legs .
Photo: YouTube/Supercar Ron Before the fourth showdown, scientific rigor required a pit stop for the drivers to swap seats, though Anderson immediately complained that Lamborghini's twin-turbo V8 sounds suspiciously like a household vacuum cleaner. He also snatched the initial jump in the white Temerario, but Supercar Ron buried his right foot in the ZR1X, reeled in the Italian exotic effortlessly, and rocketed past before the checkered cone.
The ‘Vette lived up to expectations, and to its quickly-built fame (pun intended). Bonham declared the ZR1X quicker from 0 to 160 mph than his former Bugatti Chiron, McLaren P1, and Porsche 918 Spyder, while praising the Temerario for hanging much closer than his Lamborghini Revuelto ever managed against his regular ZR1. In a defiant finale, Bonham threw down a $500 cash wager to any owner of a 1,500-horsepower modified Nissan GT-R brave enough to face his stock Bowtie king.

Cameras can show what happened on a route. Whether they help a driver avoid the next collision depends on two things: what the camera tells the driver on the road and what your safety team does with the footage afterward.
Fleet safety managers know the pattern. Footage builds up faster than anyone can review it, investigations crowd out coaching and leadership wants proof that the program is working. Adding cameras won’t solve that on its own. The fix is a clear plan for what to review, how to coach and what to measure.
Answer the four questions below to find your fleet’s video safety maturity stage, then use the guidance for that stage to choose your next step. Treat the result as a starting point for planning.
Four questions to assess your program
Choose the answer that best describes how your fleet works today.
When do you usually talk with a driver about a safety issue? Only after a collision or another incident. When we review video or telematics data to establish fault or support a claim. When in-cab voice coaching flags a behavior and a manager follows up on patterns. Before an incident occurs, when risk insights flag a driver for attention.
How does your team find safety events to review? Only after a collision or another incident. When we review video or telematics data to establish fault or support a claim. When in-cab voice coaching flags a behavior and a manager follows up on patterns. Before an incident occurs, when risk insights flag a driver for attention.
How connected is your video data to the rest of your fleet operations? Video and telematics live in separate systems, if we have telematics at all. Our cameras are cloud-connected, but we use them mainly to record evidence. Video events sit alongside engine and driving data in one platform, which gives context for coaching. Video, telematics and predictive analytics work together to estimate collision risk.
How do you show the value of your video program? We don’t measure it formally because cameras are mainly an insurance requirement. We track driver exonerations, dismissed claims and liability savings. We track changes in specific risky behaviors and completed coaching sessions. We track fleet collision rates and total cost of risk against a baseline or benchmark.
Stage 1: Reactive
Your cameras record incidents, but footage usually comes out only after something goes wrong. By then, you may be dealing with an injured driver, a damaged vehicle and an open claim. Drivers rarely get feedback outside those incidents and near-misses go unseen, so safety conversations become tied to bad news.
What moves you forward: Connectivity. Cloud-connected cameras, such as Geotab’s GO Focus Plus and GO Focus Pro , upload event footage automatically when they detect risky driving. Your team no longer has to retrieve video by hand, investigations move faster and managers can talk with drivers about a behavior before it becomes a habit.
Stage 2: Protect
You have evidence when an incident happens. That evidence can protect drivers from false accusations and your company from fraudulent claims, which is a real accomplishment.
Defending incidents still takes management time and legal effort, even when the outcome is in your favor. A program built around the aftermath also does little for the driver who has never been told they follow too closely.
What moves you forward: Feedback as it happens. Cameras with in-cab voice coaching, such as GO Focus Plus and GO Focus Pro , speak up when they detect distraction, fatigue or tailgating. Drivers can self-correct on the spot without waiting for a manager. When an alert reflects what a driver really did, the driver is more likely to accept the coaching than dispute it, and managers spend less time building cases.
Stage 3: Prevent
Drivers get coaching close to the behavior, risky events are declining and your team isn’t buried in false alerts. You’ve also built something many programs struggle with: coaching that drivers see as fair.
The next challenge is volume. As your fleet or program grows, so does the number of events. Your team needs to know which events deserve attention today and which drivers need follow-up.
What moves you forward: Prioritization. Look for software that ranks events by severity, so the most serious ones reach managers first. It should also show the key moment of each clip with speed and location, so a manager can judge an event without watching the full video. Geotab’s video platform does both. It also flags drivers whose driving patterns point to a higher chance of a collision, so managers can step in before an incident occurs.
Stage 4: Predict
Your program uses risk insights to step in before habits lead to collisions. The challenge now is proof. A collision that didn’t happen leaves no incident report or claim, so the value of that work can be hard to show to finance, leadership and insurance carriers. What moves you forward: Tracking risk over time. Keep a documented record of how your fleet’s collision risk has changed. Compare risky driving before and after coaching, using your fleet’s own history as the baseline. Then watch how driver risk changes from month to month. Geotab’s safety reporting covers both. Bring that record, along with coaching completion and total cost of risk, into conversations with leadership and carriers.
Start with one gap
Most fleets don’t fit neatly into a single stage. You may have strong evidence practices but an inconsistent coaching routine, or good coaching with no clear way to report results. Pick the area that held your answers back and work on it first. Explain to drivers
how video supports coaching, give managers a consistent review routine and track a few measures tied to your safety goals.
